summary: Port Bickerton's harbour light on Nova Scotia's Eastern Shore: lit 1901, a 1930 keeper's house now a museum, and a 1963 Coast Guard tower that is still active.

structures.type: square white tower with red top, beside a white building

structures.note: Lantern removed in 1963; a museum since 1997 (Rowlett; LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Museum and 1930 tower open daily 1 July to 30 September, admission fee (Rowlett). The 1963 Coast Guard tower: site open, tower closed (Rowlett; LighthouseFriends).

visit.note: Only the 1930 museum tower, seasonal. The 1963 Coast Guard tower is closed.

stay.note: Keeper's house rented weekly and used for an artist-in-residence programme since 2014 (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett; the station's own site).

events.note: Put in operation 10 October 1901: fixed white, 43 ft (13.1 m) above high water, visible 7 miles.
Square wooden tower, 23 ft (7 m) high, built by Emery Taylor of Stillwater for $500.
Theodore O'Hara appointed first keeper; the 1910 list gives 26 January 1901 at $205 a year (checked on the page image).
First keeper's dwelling built, so the keeper no longer rowed to and from the light.

10 April 1912: the Norwegian-registered vessel Urbye was wrecked near what the report spells 'Port Beckerton island'. A formal investigation at Halifax, 30 May, found the master at fault and reported him to the Norwegian Government for action.
New combined light and keeper's dwelling; contract awarded 28 November 1929 to Stewart C. MacMillan of Isaac's Harbour for $5,600 (LighthouseFriends); Rowlett gives 1930.
Fire from Fisherman's Harbour reached the station; residents helped fight it with seawater; minor roof damage only.
Diaphone fog alarm added; an assistant keeper assigned because of the extra work.
New one-storey keeper's dwelling built by Quemar Co. Ltd. of Bedford at a cost of $21,825.
Fog alarm building destroyed by fire on 28 March 1962 (oil-soaked floorboards ignited during paint stripping); rebuilt in concrete.
Present light tower: active, focal plane 20.5 m (Rowlett); CCG focal height 20.6 m, structure 9.2 m.
The 1930 light has been inactive since 1963 (Rowlett); its lantern was removed in 1963.
Electronic horn replaced the diaphone fog alarm.
Last keeper (Hector Lowe) left in 1988, after the light had been automated.
Opened on 28 June 1997 as the Port Bickerton Lighthouse Interpretive Centre (LighthouseFriends); Rowlett gives June 1997 as a lighthouse museum.
Site and tower transferred to the Municipality of the District of St. Mary's on 15 June 2013 (Rowlett). LighthouseFriends gives October 2012.

From 2014 the keeper's house was run as an artist residence and weekly vacation rental (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett; the station's own site). No restoration of the keeper's house is recorded in these sources.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Sources differ on whether the light is still lit. The 1963 Coast Guard tower is active and year-round (Coast Guard list; Rowlett). The 1930 lighthouse, which carried the earlier light, has been inactive since 1963 and is now a museum (Rowlett).
Rowlett gives white light 4 s on, 4 s off for the 1963 tower. The Coast Guard list gives Fl W 3s (flash 1 s, eclipse 2 s). The Coast Guard list is the current authority.

notes_for_editor: Ownership disagrees. Rowlett says the municipality owns the site and the 1963 tower (council request 2012, transfer 15 June 2013). LighthouseFriends says the transfer was in October 2012 and that the Coast Guard owns the new tower. The story reports both. The story also reports the 1997 opening under the LighthouseFriends name (Port Bickerton and Area Planning Association); Rowlett calls it a Planning Commission, and the station's own site calls itself the Port Bickerton Lighthouse Association. The story says 'a local planning body'. The wreck entry (fiscal 1912-13) spells the place 'Port Beckerton island'. Checked on the page image (printed p. 187, scan 194): the row beside the 10 April entry names the vessel Urbye (Norwegian), and a formal investigation at Halifax on 30 May found the master at fault. The story does not identify the island: LighthouseFriends does not mention this wreck, so the Bickerton Island identification is unsourced and is not used. O'Hara's appointment date (26 January 1901) was read from the OCR '1001' and checked on the page image of the 1910 list (printed p. 257, scan 259: 'Jan. 26, 1901', $205). The 1908 list (printed p. 180, scan 189) also lists him at Port Bickerton, on the image. Salary: $150 at first (LighthouseFriends) and $205 in the 1910 list; both stated. Printed pages checked on the page image: the 1901 description starts on printed p. 59 (scan 74). The quotation 'a harbour light has been established' is on printed p. 30 (scan 45) and is cited separately as source 9. Fire: LighthouseFriends says the first lighthouse was lost to fire 'in the late 1920s'; no year is given, so it is not an event in the JSON. 1947 and 1962 fire details come only from LighthouseFriends, which quotes no Department report for them; the 1962 entry is dated from LighthouseFriends. Post-1960 keepers (G. Fred Budge, Lamont Lovitt, Edgar Schraeder, Hector Lowe, and the 1960s-80s keepers generally) are named only as LighthouseFriends prints them, with no personal detail; LighthouseFriends' details about a keeper's family and a resident's role in the 1990s are left out. The 1913 keeper names in the 1916 crew list (Walter Archibald Kaiser, Port Bickerton) are seamen's certificates, not keepers, and are not used. The Marine corpus ends in 1924: the keepers after 1924 and the 1930 and 1963 works come from LighthouseFriends and Rowlett only. Rowlett gives the 1963 tower as 10 m (33 ft) and focal plane 20.5 m; the Coast Guard list gives 9.2 m structure and focal height 20.6 m; the record and story use the Coast Guard figures. The record's coordinates (45.090028, -61.700585) match the Coast Guard list (45 05 24.0 N, 061 42 01.7 W) to within about 10 m, so no correction is proposed. Newspapers: Chronicling America 'Port Bickerton' 1900 to 1930 returned 12 pages that do not concern the station. No storms chapter beyond the 1912 wreck, the 1920s fire, the 1947 fire and the 1962 fire is written. LighthouseFriends is copyrighted; the story uses its own words, and quotes from it are internal evidence only.
